content.thinking:
I need to be careful writing the postmortem, avoiding any self-generated figures and using placeholder names in braces instead. Looking at the evidence, there's a discrepancy: the admin flag toggle is logged at 11:12:42, but evaluation logs show partial rollout already happening at 11:07, with 41 of 200 evaluations seeing the flag on and the ZeroDivisionError appearing from that same 11:07 timestamp.

The revert at 11:13:54 doesn't align cleanly either -- flag-on evaluations seem to continue through 11:16, suggesting the revert may not have actually stopped the on-state evaluations, followed by another toggle back on at 11:15:59. Since the timing of the proximal cause (the ZeroDivisionError in spend_summary.py) precedes the first recorded flag change, I should be careful not to assert that the admin's action caused the onset, since the honest chain of events shows errors starting before the logged change event.

Given the revert didn't appear to restore healthy behavior within the window, I can't confirm the flag toggle alone resolved the issue, so I need to hedge in how I state the root cause -- framing it as a code path triggered when the flag evaluates true, but noting the causal link to the specific admin action is uncertain.

For the write-up, I'll use the duration placeholder for how long things were broken, incorporate the error count placeholders for before/during/worst periods, and since there aren't existing action items, I'll draft a set of new ones labeled sequentially.

Drafting the action items now: one for a staged rollout with automatic rollback tied to error-rate monitoring plus a test for the zero-division case, one specifically for fixing the division-by-zero bug itself with a regression test, one for improving detection by better aligning flag-change timestamps with evaluation logs and alerting on error correlation per flag, and one process item investigating why the revert didn't actually take effect -- possibly a flag-provider propagation or caching issue -- along with tightening how revert success gets verified before declaring it ineffective.

I'm also noting the detection gap between when the issue began and when the alert fired, which ties back into the detection improvement item, and preparing the causal chain with citations: the user-facing error spike, the ZeroDivisionError at the specific line, the flag evaluating "on" for part of traffic from onset, and the admin's switch-on action with its timestamp.

But the change record timestamp postdates the log evidence of the flag already being active, which is unexplained and worth flagging with citations. The revert itself didn't stop the issue (evaluations continued afterward per the evidence), so I'm treating that as a "went wrong" item rather than part of the causal chain, keeping the root cause focused on the ungated divide-by-zero path being enabled for live traffic — and noting as a positive that the response from alert to action happened within about a minute.

I'm also considering what "got lucky" items to include: the failure only affected a portion of traffic with flat latency, and the error trace included an exact file and line number making the fix location obvious. I need to watch for stray digits in the write-up, like line numbers, since those read as figures I should avoid stating directly.

action_items.item: Roll out flags to a small share of traffic first, with an automatic rollback if the error rate of the gated path rises above baseline.
Fix the division by zero in spend_summary.py, add a test for the zero-denominator input, and require that test before the flag is enabled again.

Find out why the error rate stayed high after monthly-spend-feature was switched off. Check the flag provider's propagation and caching, and the evaluations logged as on after the revert. Make Argus verify that evaluations have flipped before it judges a flag revert.
Record the flag's change time and the per-flag evaluation split from the same clock, and alert on errors that correlate with a flag's on evaluations so detection is not later than onset.

Give the escalation a handover note for the on-call engineer. It should say that the flag was reverted without effect and then restored, and give the live state of the flag and the options to disable the gated code path directly or roll back the release.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw account page requests fail. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average, peaking at {errors_at_worst}, from {began}, and had not recovered by the last minute read.

The failing requests threw a ZeroDivisionError in spend_summary.py. These errors began at the onset and continued through the last minute read. Disconnects by shoppers were a separate, small background of errors.

That code ran because the monthly-spend-feature flag evaluated as on. It was on for a minority of evaluations at the onset, then for every evaluation. Before that, the flag was off and account pages rendered normally.

The flag had been switched on by an admin, and nothing staged or checked the path that it enabled. The change record is timestamped after the errors began, so the exact enablement time is not settled by the record.

Argus switched the flag off and waited, but the error rate was not back at baseline and the action was judged refuted. Evaluations of the flag as on were still logged through the last minute read. The record does not show why the errors continued, so the chain stops here.

contributing_factors.factor: The flag's code path was enabled for live traffic without a zero-denominator case being tested, and without a staged rollout that stops when errors rise.

The revert did not restore baseline and the record cannot say why. Evaluations of the flag as on continued, and Argus judged the action without confirming that the flag had actually flipped for the service.
The change record for the flag is timestamped after the first errors and the first on evaluations. The alert fired after onset. The change history cannot be lined up reliably with the onset.
After the revert was refuted and the second investigation found no new cause, Argus left the flag on with the fault live. It escalated with no further mitigation.

input.executive_summary: From {began}, a large share of account page requests on io-shop failed. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average and peaked at {errors_at_worst}. It had not recovered by the last metrics read, so shoppers were affected for at least {duration}. The errors were a division-by-zero in the code behind the monthly-spend-feature flag, which was on for the affected requests. Argus switched the flag off, but the error rate did not return to baseline. It judged the action refuted and put the flag back on. A second investigation found nothing new, so Argus escalated to people. The incident was held by Argus for {held}. It is not resolved, and the cause of the continued errors after the revert is unexplained.

got_lucky: The log line named the failing file and the division by zero, which gives engineers a concrete place to start the fix.
Only the requests that evaluated the flag as on failed. Latency stayed flat, so the damage did not spread to the rest of the service.
went_well: Argus took the alert up, formed a candidate and acted on it quickly. It read metrics, changes, logs and flag history in a single pass.
Argus used its memory of an earlier incident, where putting the same flag back did not help, to move that action down the list on the second pass. It then escalated rather than repeat the action.
went_wrong: The one mitigation tried, reverting the flag, did not restore baseline, and the service was still broken at the last minute read.
The second investigation produced a candidate that restated the first, and one that was speculative. The cause of the lasting errors was not found.
The alert fired after the onset, and the flag change record does not line up with the first errors.

input.root_cause: The code path gated by the monthly-spend-feature flag divides by zero in spend_summary.py, so every account page request that evaluated the flag as on failed. The flag was enabled for live traffic with no staged check or automatic rollback. Switching it off did not restore baseline within the window read, so the flag being the whole cause is not proven.
input.symptom: Account pages failed for many shoppers
